newsitem.title: INDIA: India not to alter buying pattern on crude oil dip.
newsitem.headline: India not to alter buying pattern on crude oil dip.

text.p: India, faced with a ballooning oil bill, is not expected to change its purchasing strategy with the recent slide in world crude prices but the drop has given it some breathing space, officials and analysts said on Wednesday.
"I don't think they will change the strategy of buying," said Rajendra Pachouri, director of the independent Tata Energy Research Institute (TERI).
"This (fall in prices) is something that has come as a pleasant surprise," Pachouri told Reuters.

Analysts said world crude prices started falling in the past four weeks and are currently quoted in the range of $17-19 per barrel in different markets. Oil prices had reached a peak of $26 per barrel in October-November 1996.

Traders in Singapore said they would not expect the recent price slide to change IOC's buying patterns because term contract prices are usually reviewed each month and follow the trend of the spot market.
As crude prices fall, so will the official selling price (OSP) of the country with which IOC has term deals.
"They would not benefit more from spot than term when prices are falling," one trader said.

IOC does not buy crude on the spot market except through a monthly tender. At the monthly tender it usually buys four or five cargoes of Dubai crude (500,000 barrels each) and two or three very large crude carriers (VLCCs) of West African crude oil. Each VLCC contains between 1.9 and 2.0 million barrels.
Despite the fall in crude prices India has increased the proportion of crude it buys on term contract. Last week India agreed to buy 3.6 million barrels of Iraqi crude over 90 days.
Traders said the Iraq term agreement could impact India's appetite for Dubai crude oil through the monthly crude buying tenders. Iraqi crude would compete with Dubai.
IOC officials at New Delhi said even when they buy on term there was no fixed rate.
They said in term contracts an average was worked out on the basis of the rates that prevail three days prior to loading and three days after loading to ensure neither party was disadvantaged.
Pachouri said the decline in crude prices was a reflection of a relatively mild winter in North America and parts of Europe and Iraq's entry as an oil exporter.
Indian petroleum ministry officials said the country would gain from the fall in international prices.
"India's oil pool deficit will not grow at the rapid rate at which it was growing following the drop in prices," said one IOC official.
India's oil pool deficit -- effectively the amount the government owes oil companies for selling products well below world prices -- will hit 158 billion rupees ($4.4 billion) by the end of March.
"Even though oil prices have come down, so long as they don't come below $15 per barrel the oil pool deficit will keep increasing," said Sanjeev Patni of securities firm W.I. Carr.
Patni said in an ideal situation like this India should have been buying and stocking crude, but oil companies are not awash in funds and have even reached their borrowing limits.
India's crude oil output in 1996/97 (April-March) is forecast at around 34 million tonnes, down from 35.19 million in 1995/96.
The country's demand for petroleum products is forecast to go up to about 81 million tonnes in the year ending March 31, 1997 from 74.7 million in 1995/96.
Pachouri said India had comfortable crude stocks. "My guess is about 30 to 40 days of stocks."
There are wide price variations in this category and Keskar did not give the actual numbers of medium-sized airliners he expected to be delivered.
The small-sized aircraft segment, like Boeing's 737 series, will see 29 percent growth in the region, involving the delivery of some 100 new aircraft and expenditure of around $5.0 billion, he said.

Deliveries of large aircraft, like Boeing's 747-400s, to the region will grow 13 percent over the period, involving around 15 aircraft at a cost of $2.0 billion. Boeing expects Air India to be its main regional customer for jumbo-jets.

The aircraft maker expects to maintain close relations with Air India, Indian Airlines and private airlines such as Jet Airways, Sahara India Airlines, SKyline NEPC and Modiluft, Keskar said in press statement.
He said Boeing's 737 was the preferred and only choice of private jet operators in India. It expects its next generation 737-600 to be Indian Airlines' choice to replace its 737-200s.
Keskar also expected the 767 and 777 series to fulfil Indian Airlines' demand for 300-seater planes.
Keskar said he was confident that Air India will opt for the Boeing 777 as its medium-capacity, long-range airplane.
